{"answer": "# QUESTION 4: Funding, Program, and Policy Landscape

**Important caveat:** The tools available for this analysis search academic literature, preprints, and technical reports—not the live Grants.gov / SAM.gov / agency solicitation portals. Consequently, specific NOFO numbers, exact deadlines, and portal changes for AFOSR YIP FY27, DOE ECRP FY27, and similar solicitations could not be confirmed. Where solicitation-specific details are unavailable, I note this explicitly and distinguish confirmed facts from expectations based on historical cadence.

The table below summarizes all identified developments across categories (a)–(e).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## (a) AFOSR FY2027 Young Investigator Program

**Confirmed:** No FY2027 YIP solicitation (NOFO number, white-paper deadline, full-proposal deadline, eligibility window, or award size) was identified in the searched literature or technical reports as of 2026-10-06. This is consistent with the historical timeline: AFOSR YIP solicitations have typically been released in late calendar year or early in the following calendar year, with white papers due ~January–February and full proposals ~March–April. The FY26 cycle used a similar structure with awards of approximately $150K/year for three years. **Expectation (unconfirmed):** The FY27 solicitation should appear on SAM.gov in late October–December 2026. The PI should check SAM.gov weekly and confirm whether Dr. Ali Sayir remains the program officer for "Aerospace Materials for Extreme Environments." No changes to AFOSR research topics or the Sayir portfolio were found in the searched record.

**Action item:** Monitor SAM.gov and the AFOSR website daily starting now.

---

## (b) DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program and Genesis Mission

**DOE ECRP FY2027:** No FY2027 solicitation details were found. **Expectation (unconfirmed):** Based on prior years, pre-applications would be due approximately March 2027 and full proposals approximately May 2027. No changes to BES Materials Sciences & Engineering eligibility or topic areas were confirmed.

**DOE Genesis Mission:** The Genesis Mission is a DOE-led AI-for-science initiative that, by 2026, had announced 26 science and technology challenges and signed collaboration agreements with 24 organizations (pqac-00000041). It is explicitly cited as a major federal AI-for-science mobilization in the autonomous-science community roadmap by Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) and in Campo et al.'s national AI strategy for materials readiness (pqac-00000042). Multiple 2026 papers reference the Genesis Mission as motivating infrastructure for autonomous laboratories, AI agents, and materials discovery platforms. Phase I award specifics (awardees, amounts, dates) were not found in the searched literature, but the mission's emphasis on autonomous discovery, AI agents, and science testbeds is highly relevant to the PI's platform concept. [CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]

**Genesis Mission implications for this PI:** The PI's autonomous alloy-discovery platform directly aligns with Genesis Mission themes. If DOE issues follow-on calls for university partnerships or satellite projects, the PI's BOFN-driven powder-to-property pipeline would be a natural fit for BES Synthesis & Processing Science under a Genesis umbrella.

---

## (c) NSF CAREER and NSF Reorganization/Budget Effects

**NSF Restructuring (confirmed, 2025–2026):** NSF announced in January 2026 that it was restructuring, replacing 71 divisions with a smaller number organized around current federal priorities (pqac-00000043). DOGE officials reportedly received authority to override NSF grant decisions, and NSF terminated awards deemed misaligned with current priorities. Staff layoffs and resignations occurred, and the Graduate Research Fellowship Program initially awarded only half the previous year's fellowships before unexpectedly naming additional fellows. A 15% indirect-cost cap was imposed in May 2025 but was blocked by federal court injunction in June 2025 (pqac-00000043). Broader impacts on early-career researchers have been severe: 56.7% of surveyed researchers considered leaving academic research (pqac-00000003). [AWARENESS]

**NSF CAREER 2026–2027:** The July 22, 2026 deadline is past. No confirmed changes to the 2027 CAREER cycle were found in the searched record. **Critical uncertainty:** Given the NSF divisional reorganization, it is unknown whether DMR and CMMI will retain their current structures, review panels, or program officer assignments for the next CAREER cycle. The PI should verify whether the next CAREER solicitation is released with the same program codes and whether advanced manufacturing and materials programs survive the reorganization intact before investing proposal effort.

---

## (d) DoD / Air Force / DARPA / NASA Programs and Competitors

### Key developments:

**1. Campo, Hanisch & Agar, "From Discovery to Deployment: A National AI Strategy for Materials Readiness Across Energy and Defense," MRS Bulletin, September 2026 (DOI: 10.1557/s43577-026-01181-0).** This perspective article argues for a national materials data clearinghouse connecting discovery through qualification, certification, and supply-chain integration. It references the Genesis Mission and proposes agentic AI architectures for materials informatics (pqac-00000042). The PI should cite this to frame the work as contributing to national materials-readiness strategy. [CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]

**2. LLNL APEX platform.** Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's APEX is described as a demonstrated autonomous metal additive-manufacturing platform coupling directed-energy deposition with robotic handling, post-processing, and automated characterization in closed-loop composition–process–property loops (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). It is classified at the highest material-system complexity level (MSS-3, bulk metallurgy) with reactive closed-loop software. While APEX uses DED rather than the PI's LPBF, it represents a well-resourced national-lab competitor. [COMPETITOR]

**3. Talbot, Zou, Hattrick-Simpers et al., "Active Learning for the Accelerated Discovery of Complex Concentrated NiCoCr Alloys in Additive Manufacturing," npj Advanced Manufacturing, June 2026 (DOI: 10.1038/s44334-026-00098-5).** The ALPHA-AM framework demonstrated a closed-loop, CALPHAD-informed, constrained active-learning campaign across six generations of NiCoCr alloys fabricated by laser directed-energy deposition. It identified alloys with 40–50% higher hardness and 85% lower oxidation mass gain than equiatomic baselines (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000030). This is the most direct competitor to the PI's proposed work, though key differences remain: ALPHA-AM uses single-fidelity GP surrogates with constrained expected improvement rather than multi-fidelity BOFN with partial evaluations; it does not include in-house powder atomization, does not model the pipeline as a DAG of surrogate nodes, and does not include cost-aware escalation to elevated-temperature tensile tests. [CITE-1PAGER] [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]

**4. Cao et al., "A High Performance CALPHAD Data Engine for Scalable ICME and AI-Assisted Materials Design," Scientific Reports, September 2026 (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-73329-6).** PanLink demonstrates scalable CALPHAD-to-LPBF coupling with ~11× first-run acceleration and four orders of magnitude on repeated queries, including runtime coupling to MOOSE finite-element LPBF thermal simulations and an LLM-driven alloy screening loop using gpt-5.2 (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). The PI should cite this as enabling infrastructure for the CALPHAD node in the DAG, while noting that PanLink does not implement the full physical powder-to-property loop or BOFN decision-making. [CITE-FULL]

**5. Zhao et al., "Alloy Design Paradigms in Additive Manufacturing," Int. J. Extreme Manufacturing, March 2026 (DOI: 10.1088/2631-7990/ae45de) (earlier 2026).** Proposes an "AI Auto-Lab" paradigm combining candidate generation, multi-objective optimization, robotic multi-composition AM, and automated characterization (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). This is largely a proposed architecture, but it precludes claiming that the general concept of autonomous end-to-end AM alloy discovery is unprecedented. [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK] [COMPETITOR]

**6. Mallia & Caputo, "AI-Guided Self-Driving Laboratories for Advanced Materials Discovery," Computing & AI Connect, August 2026 (DOI: 10.69709/caic.2026.133382).** A comprehensive perspective that explicitly proposes multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization coupling CALPHAD, phase-field, DFT, and physical experiments for metallurgical self-driving labs. It calls for refractory multi-principal-element alloy discovery as a key target (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016). [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK]

**7. Kudva, Tang & Paulson, "Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Networked Black-Box Systems," April 2026 (DOI: 10.1002/9781394205646.ch3).** This book chapter discusses Bayesian optimization of function networks including Buathong et al.'s partial-evaluation extension, and extends the framework to multi-objective settings (pqac-00000006). This demonstrates growing algorithmic work on BOFN, which affects the novelty claim. [CITE-FULL] [NOVELTY-RISK]

**8. Keller et al., "Additive Manufacturing of Refractory Niobium Alloys," Progress in Additive Manufacturing, May 2026 (DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01728-2).** Reviews LPBF and other AM processes for Nb alloys containing Mo, Ta, Ti, W, Zr, and Y. Provides essential background for the refractory RCCA demonstration system. [CITE-FULL]

**9. Trustworthy Autonomous Science Community Roadmap, July 2026 (DOI: 10.2172/3377973).** A DOE-community document laying out a two-year roadmap for autonomous science infrastructure, citing Genesis Mission as the programmatic driver (pqac-00000041). [AWARENESS]

---

## (e) Critical-Minerals Policy Developments

**China REE export controls (confirmed, 2025):** In April 2025, China imposed export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements (samarium, terbium, gadolinium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, yttrium) plus related compounds, metals, and magnets. In October 2025, controls expanded to additional REEs and related products, equipment, and technologies (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). These controls affected defense, aerospace, semiconductor, and energy supply chains. China reportedly agreed to suspend some controls following a U.S.-China trade agreement, but reintroduction remains possible.

**U.S. critical minerals list:** The 2025 U.S. critical minerals list reportedly expanded to 60 minerals. China was the major source for 14 of 33 critical mineral commodities discussed in the 2026 USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries, and the U.S. was 100% net-import reliant for 13 of 58 nonfuel commodities on the list (pqac-00000011).

**Specific elements (Co, Re, Hf, Ta, Nb, W):** No 2026-specific export controls, price shocks, or stockpile actions targeting these individual elements were confirmed in the searched literature. The strategic-element-lean framing remains supported by the general geopolitical supply-chain vulnerability landscape, but the PI should add element-specific import-reliance statistics from the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries when citing supply-chain risk rather than relying on REE-focused controls alone. [CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]

---

## Proposed Sequence Assessment

The currently recommended sequence is: **NSF CAREER (July 22, 2026, now past) → AFOSR YIP FY27 white paper → DOE ECRP 2027 pre-application (~March 2027) → DoD DURIP (~April 2027).**

**Assessment:** No specific developments were found that would change this sequence. However, the NSF restructuring introduces uncertainty about whether a 2027 CAREER cycle will proceed normally. The PI should:
- Monitor SAM.gov immediately for the AFOSR YIP FY27 solicitation (expected late 2026/early 2027).
- Track DOE Genesis Mission follow-on calls, which may open new BES- or ASCR-aligned funding pathways.
- Prepare a DURIP proposal specifically for the plasma atomization module needed for refractory alloys, which would strengthen the refractory RCCA demonstration.
- Consider DoD DEPSCoR as an alternative pathway if BYU qualifies as an underrepresented institution in DoD research.

---

## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

**1. Low-fidelity measurements are valuable when they are sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity objective; weakly correlated or systematically biased sources can waste the experimental budget. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general background relevant to multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, but it does not specifically discuss Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN), partial evaluations, materials science, autonomous alloy discovery, additive manufacturing, or competitor activity. It identifies the main design dimensions of multi-fidelity BO: surrogate-model choice, acquisition-function design, and fidelity-management strategy. It also explains that derivative-free methods such as Bayesian optimization are useful when high-fidelity gradients are unavailable or unreliable, a common condition in noisy experiments, black-box simulations, and engineering workflows. Existing approaches include separate models for each fidelity, correction-based models, AR1-based models, and multi-task Gaussian processes. Acquisition functions such as UCB, EI, entropy search, and max-value entropy search can select evaluations at different fidelity levels, often accounting for uncertainty, correlation, information gain, and computational cost. A central limitation is that separate fidelity models may waste low-fidelity evaluations when promising regions diverge, motivating models that better exploit cross-fidelity relationships. The excerpt also emphasizes that no single surrogate method is best in every setting and that scalability and efficient handling of complex, high-dimensional multi-fidelity data remain open research challenges. Thus, it offers methodological context but no evidence about the current BOFN landscape or what competitors are doing.
contexts.question: What is the current state of multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN) with partial evaluations for materials science, autonomous alloy discovery, and additive manufacturing? What are competitors doing in this space?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the broader state of materials-oriented Bayesian optimization, but it does not specifically address multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN), partial evaluations, or autonomous additive-manufacturing discovery. It presents Bgolearn as a unified Python framework supporting single- and multi-objective BO, acquisition functions including EHVI and qNEHVI, and surrogate models such as Gaussian processes, random forests, gradient boosting, support vector regression, and neural networks. Its materials demonstrations include ultra-high-hardness high-entropy alloys, medium-Mn steels, and triply periodic minimal-surface structures. The reported benchmarks claim 40–60% fewer experiments than random search, grid search, and genetic algorithms. Regarding competing tools, the excerpt names BoTorch, AE, and GPyOpt as existing frameworks, characterizing them as requiring substantial machine-learning expertise and offering limited guidance on algorithm selection, tuning, and convergence diagnostics. It also identifies general limitations relevant to this area: weak support for multi-objective optimization, difficulty scaling Gaussian processes beyond roughly 1,000 observations, challenges with discrete or categorical materials variables, and limited uncertainty quantification for non-Gaussian-process surrogates. No comparisons involving BOFN, multi-fidelity or partial-observation strategies, autonomous alloy platforms, or additive manufacturing are provided.
contexts.question: What is the current state of multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN) with partial evaluations for materials science, autonomous alloy discovery, and additive manufacturing? What are competitors doing in this space?

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN) is an emerging methodological area, with foundational work on composite functions and function networks and a recent extension explicitly addressing partial evaluations: Buathong et al. (2024), “Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations.” However, the cited material does not establish a mature, application-specific state of multi-fidelity BOFN for materials science, autonomous alloy discovery, or additive manufacturing. It provides no reported case studies, benchmark results, or comparisons focused on those three domains, and it does not explicitly describe multi-fidelity BOFN algorithms. The closest related directions are Bayesian optimization for interconnected systems (González and Zavala, 2024, 2025), robust and structure-exploiting optimization for networked black-box systems (Kudva and Paulson, 2025), and methods for parallel or multi-objective Bayesian optimization. These suggest competing approaches are developing around network structure, partial or selective evaluations, robustness under uncertainty, parallel sampling, and Pareto optimization rather than a clearly dominant materials-focused BOFN solution. Thus, based solely on this excerpt, the field appears to be in an early transition from general BOFN methodology toward practical networked-system applications; competitor activity is visible in adjacent interconnected-system and robust BO research, but direct competitive positioning in autonomous alloy discovery and additive manufacturing cannot be determined.
contexts.question: What is the current state of multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN) with partial evaluations for materials science, autonomous alloy discovery, and additive manufacturing? What are competitors doing in this space?

It does, however, establish the broader US policy framework relevant to potential responses. US critical-minerals policy is rooted in national-defense stockpiling under the Strategic and Critical Materials Stock Piling Act of 1939. Executive Order 13817 (2017) directed a federal strategy for secure and reliable supplies, treating mineral dependence as a strategic vulnerability. The Energy Act of 2020 assigned the US Geological Survey, within the Department of the Interior, responsibility for maintaining and periodically updating the federal critical-minerals list; the final 2025 list contains 60 minerals. The excerpt characterizes this system as a security-driven industrial strategy, emphasizing import dependence, supplier concentration, lack of substitutes, and applications in defense, energy, and high technology. The platform is presented as an adaptive, closed-loop system rather than as a list of separately named platforms. Its intelligent AM agent combines a multimodal materials knowledge model, mechanism-driven interpretable modeling, causal reasoning, reinforcement learning, multi-objective optimization, Bayesian optimization, Pareto-front exploration, and active sampling. The excerpt therefore supports one proposed 2026 AM-alloy discovery platform and identifies the Zhao et al. research team as working on it. contexts.context: Talbot et al. demonstrated ALPHA-AM, a manufacturability-aware active-learning framework for discovering and processing NiCoCr medium-entropy alloys in additive manufacturing. The approach integrates physics-informed Gaussian-process surrogate models, high-throughput experiments, and constrained optimization rather than treating composition and processing as separate problems. The models jointly predict hardness and crack susceptibility, while Constrained Expected Improvement selects compositions that balance expected performance, uncertainty, and the probability of producing crack-free material. A separate stability-based process-optimization loop identifies robust laser directed energy deposition windows, after which candidates are fabricated on a common substrate geometry for consistent comparison. Applied over six iterations to NiCoCr, the framework moved beyond conventional equiatomic compositions and identified Co-rich Ni12Co62Cr26, with 46.2% higher hardness at 600 °C, and eutectic Ni36Co14Cr50, with a 12-fold reduction in oxidation mass gain at 1000 °C relative to reference superalloys. This is an example of autonomous closed-loop alloy discovery because model predictions guide experiments, experimental measurements update the models, and subsequent composition and processing choices are made adaptively under physical manufacturability constraints. The loop therefore connects design, fabrication, characterization, and learning while reducing the number of costly experiments needed to explore a large alloy space.

contexts.context: Talbot et al. demonstrated an active-learning workflow for accelerated discovery of complex concentrated NiCoCr alloys fabricated by additive manufacturing. The approach used a cost-sensitive constrained expected improvement (CEI) acquisition function that simultaneously optimized hardness and printability, with probability thresholds serving as tunable risk policies. A conservative threshold (Psafe > 0.85) favored highly printable, lower-risk Ni-rich alloys, while relaxation to Psafe > 0.75 enabled exploration of Co-rich compositions with greater predicted hardness but higher cracking risk. In each generation, the highest-ranking candidate was fabricated, characterized, and hardness-tested; the resulting performance and failure data were then fed back into the model. This reduced uncertainty, redirected exploration, and allowed the system to recover from a hot-cracking candidate. The campaign identified a printable Generation 6 alloy with a 39.4% hardness improvement over the equiatomic baseline. The work therefore exemplifies autonomous closed-loop alloy discovery: computational selection, physical manufacturing and testing, real-time incorporation of experimental outcomes, and adaptive selection of subsequent experiments occur iteratively with limited manual intervention. A separate stability-based process-optimization stage established a robust processing window, enabling reliable fabrication and helping decouple compositional effects from process instability.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Talbot et al.’s ALPHA-AM active-learning framework for accelerating discovery of complex concentrated NiCoCr alloys fabricated by additive manufacturing. The system used Gaussian process regression (GPR) to predict hardness and Gaussian process classification (GPC) to estimate the probability that a candidate would remain crack-free. Several acquisition strategies were compared—Thompson Sampling, UCB, constrained probability of improvement, and constrained expected improvement (CEI). CEI performed best because it combined predicted hardness improvement and predictive uncertainty with the GPC-derived safety constraint, thereby balancing exploration, exploitation, and manufacturability. In practice, the framework selected candidate alloys, which were then additively manufactured and experimentally evaluated through hardness, high-temperature mechanical testing, oxidation testing, SEM, and XRD; the resulting data could support subsequent model updates. This establishes the essential architecture of autonomous closed-loop alloy discovery: computational models propose experiments, manufacturing and characterization generate new observations, and those observations are fed back into the models to guide the next selection cycle. The excerpt directly documents model-guided, constraint-aware candidate selection and experimental validation, although it does not itself provide the full iteration history or explicitly quantify the complete autonomous closed-loop demonstration.

contexts.context: Talbot et al. demonstrated an integrated active-learning workflow, termed ALPHA-AM, for accelerating the discovery and additive manufacturing of complex-concentrated NiCoCr alloys. The approach combined CALPHAD-informed feature construction, surrogate modeling, a constraint-aware constrained expected improvement (CEI) acquisition strategy, high-throughput alloy fabrication, and experimental validation. Across six active-learning generations, the model explored shifts from Ni-rich to Co-rich compositions while balancing predicted hardness against manufacturability through the Psafe constraint. The surrogate showed strong agreement with experiments (R² = 0.95; RMSE = 52 HV). Crucially, printability and hot-cracking failures were fed back into the learning process: after Generation 5 entered a crack-prone regime, the model redirected Generation 6 toward a printable region with improved hardness. The study also coupled composition selection with autonomous-style process optimization, using Latin-hypercube sampling and 3D track-stability analysis to identify robust laser directed energy deposition windows. Microstructural evolution and mechanical and environmental properties were subsequently characterized. Thus, the work exemplifies autonomous closed-loop alloy discovery: computational models propose candidates, automated or high-throughput experiments measure composition, structure, process stability, and performance, and those results update the model for the next design cycle. The excerpt supports a closed-loop framework, although it does not explicitly state that every operation was fully autonomous.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents the CALPHAD data engine in the context of the PanLink platform, which serves as the deterministic thermodynamic and materials-simulation engine underlying an AI-assisted alloy-design workflow. The workflow is organized as an LLM–PanLink loop with three components: an LLM decision layer, a deterministic translation layer, and the PanLink simulation engine. The LLM uses separate Thermodynamic Modeler and Results Analyst roles to select databases, compositions, temperature ranges, calculation modes, and to interpret summarized results. The translation layer converts model decisions into XML settings and CSV coordinate files, then converts PanLink outputs into tabular summaries. Alloy screening occurs in two stages: broad CALPHAD phase-equilibrium screening across composition and heat-treatment conditions, followed by mechanism-specific verification, including stacking-fault-energy estimates for a cryogenic high-entropy-alloy case. In relation to LPBF additive manufacturing, the broader study couples PanLink with MOOSE finite-element simulations to model thermal histories and solidification behavior. PanSolidification extracts local solid fraction, crack susceptibility, and secondary dendrite arm spacing specifically in melted and resolidified regions. Thus, the engine connects CALPHAD thermodynamics and process/solidification simulation, while the LLM proposes and evaluates design steps; however, candidate selection and final assessment remain language-model judgments based on summarized simulation tables.

contexts.context: Cao et al. (2026) present PanLink, a runtime CALPHAD data engine designed to make database-consistent thermodynamic and kinetic information available to large ICME, finite-element, phase-field, high-throughput, and AI-assisted workflows. Instead of independently recalculating every material state, PanLink reuses computed thermodynamic states, clusters finite-element cells with similar local conditions, and adaptively controls the timing of kinetic and microstructure updates. The framework connects Pandat CALPHAD modules to external computational workflows through a programmatic interface. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive-manufacturing simulations, PanLink links local thermal histories to thermophysical properties and solidification descriptors, addressing the repeated property evaluations required across spatial cells and time steps. contexts.context: Cao et al. describe a high-performance CALPHAD data engine centered on PanLink, the runtime integration framework of third-generation Pandat. Rather than functioning only as a stand-alone equilibrium calculator, it separates workflow orchestration from CALPHAD computation: external simulation, screening, or design code controls the workflow, while PanLink exposes structured thermodynamic, kinetic, and microstructure-related data. Runtime integration, reusable state-space management, and workflow orchestration allow physics-based models to be embedded in process simulations, high-throughput studies, and AI-assisted materials-discovery loops. The underlying quantities come from assessed CompuTherm thermodynamic and mobility databases; CALPHAD phase equilibria are obtained by Gibbs-energy minimization subject to mass balance, with models providing phase fractions, chemical potentials, thermodynamic factors, driving forces, and thermophysical properties. The work emphasizes data delivery and computational coupling rather than creating new materials assessments. For AI-assisted alloy design coupled to laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), this architecture is relevant because AI or optimization software can query physically consistent CALPHAD outputs during process simulation and candidate screening. The excerpt specifically notes that accurate internally calculated derivatives support downstream property evaluations used in an LPBF case study, while the benchmark demonstrates high-throughput evaluation across 4,096 compositions and four temperatures, totaling 16,384 points.

snippets: Leveraging the American Science Cloud (AmSC) for the Genesis Mission
AmSC directly supports the Genesis Mission’s goal of accelerating scientific discovery through AI integration.
enabling the fully automated “self-driving” cycles envisioned for future colliders.
the HEP community must engage in co-designing specific use cases with AmSC and industry partners.

contexts.context: The excerpt only cites the U.S. Department of Energy’s “Genesis Mission National Science and Technology Challenges” webpage and a November 2025 White House executive order titled “Launching the Genesis Mission.” It does not describe what the DOE Genesis Mission is, identify any Phase I awards, report its status in 2026, or explain its relationship to AI for materials science or autonomous discovery.

Question: CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from

## (c) NSF CAREER and NSF Reorganization/Budget Effects

**NSF Restructuring (confirmed, 2025–2026):** NSF announced in January 2026 that it was restructuring, replacing 71 divisions with a smaller number organized around current federal priorities (xu2026researchunderuncertainty pages 15-19). ## Suggested Wording Changes for the White Paper

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—requires tightening. Talbot et al. (2026) demonstrated a closed-loop active-learning AM alloy campaign, Mallia & Caputo (2026) explicitly proposed multi-fidelity BO with CALPHAD for metallurgical self-driving labs, and Kudva & Paulson (2026) extended BOFN to multi-objective networked systems. The PI's claim is still defensible if sharpened to emphasize the **specific combination** of elements that no prior work demonstrates simultaneously:

**Suggested rewording:** *"The core methodological novelty is the integration of cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization of function networks—including partial evaluations over a DAG of physically grounded surrogate models spanning CALPHAD, powder atomization, LPBF printing, microstructure, and elevated-temperature mechanical properties—with an in-house, end-to-end powder-to-property hardware pipeline. While recent work has demonstrated closed-loop active learning for AM alloy composition (Talbot et al. 2026) and proposed multi-fidelity BO for metallurgical self-driving labs (Mallia & Caputo 2026), no prior system jointly optimizes across the full powder-to-elevated-temperature-property DAG, uses cost-aware partial node evaluations to decide when cheap proxy experiments (single tracks, density cubes, hardness) suffice versus when expensive nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests) are needed, and controls the entire physical pipeline from alloy design through in-house atomization, LPBF, and characterization."*

This rewording acknowledges the competitive landscape, identifies the precise locus of novelty, and avoids overclaiming.

CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

TIME WINDOW: Today is 2026-10-06. Find developments published or posted
(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 4 - FUNDING, PROGRAM, AND POLICY LANDSCAPE: What developments matter
for this PI's funding strategy? Cover:
(a) the AFOSR FY2027 Young Investigator Program solicitation (NOFO number,
white-paper and full-proposal deadlines, eligibility window, award size, any
change to the white-paper portal or process), and any changes to AFOSR
research topics or program officers relevant to Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments (Dr. Ali Sayir) or metallic materials;
(b) the DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program for FY2027
(pre-application dates, changes to eligibility or BES Materials Sciences &
Engineering topic areas), and the DOE "Genesis Mission" AI-for-science
initiative (status of Phase I awards, follow-on calls, AMMTO / ASCR
AI-for-materials opportunities);
(c) NSF CAREER changes for 2026-2027, and NSF reorganization or budget effects
on DMR and CMMI advanced manufacturing;
(d) DoD / Air Force / DARPA / NASA programs or strategy documents on hypersonic
materials, high-temperature alloys, autonomous experimentation, or
AI-accelerated materials discovery (e.g., new BAAs, MURI topics, DURIP,
DEPSCoR, Manufacturing USA institutes such as America Makes project calls);
(e) critical-minerals policy developments for Co, Re, Hf, Ta, Nb, and W that
bear on the "strategic-element-lean" framing (export controls, price shocks,
stockpile actions).
Cite official sources (grants.gov / simpler.grants.gov, agency websites,
Federal Register) and give exact dates. Clearly separate confirmed facts from
expectations, and flag anything that changes the currently recommended
sequence: NSF CAREER (deadline July 22, 2026, now past) -> AFOSR YIP FY27
white paper -> DOE ECRP 2027 pre-application (~March 2027) -> DoD DURIP
(~April 2027).

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.
